chunks: Ball grid array packages and trade-offs. The question: What are ball grid array (BGA) packages? What are their tradeoffs?
A ball grid array, or BGA, is a chip package whose connections are small solder balls laid out in a grid on its underside, instead of legs around the edge.
The grid fits many connections into a small area and keeps each path short. The price is hidden joints and a board that needs careful design.
Picture a crowd standing in a grid on a floor, each person needing a path to the exit. The people at the edge walk out easily. People in the middle need gaps to squeeze through.
Pack them tighter and the gaps vanish. A BGA board is the same: every ball needs a path, and tighter spacing leaves less room.
A BGA is a die on a small multilayer substrate whose underside carries a grid of solder balls that mate with pads on the PCB.
The red bar marks the distance from the package centre: the farther a ball is, the more the thermal mismatch between substrate and board shears it, so corner balls are the weakest.
Pitch: the center-to-center spacing between neighboring balls. Reflow: heating the board so the balls and solder paste melt and form joints.
Escape routing: getting a copper path from each ball out to the edge of the grid or down to another board layer.
Via: a tiny plated hole that connects copper on different layers of the board. X-ray inspection: the way to check hidden joints, since nothing is visible from above.
Take a 10 mm square package with balls at 0. 5 mm pitch. The grid is 20 times 20, so it holds 400 balls. An edge-pin package of the same size and pitch holds only about 80 pins.
That is the density win. Now the routing. At 0. 8 mm pitch with pads half that size, the gap between pads is 0. 4 mm. A 0. 1 mm copper path (a trace) needs 0.
1 mm of clearance on each side, so 0. 3 mm total, and it fits. At 0. 5 mm pitch the gap is only 0. 25 mm, so it does not fit.
You then put a via inside the pad itself, which costs more. That is the whole idea.
"A BGA has solder balls in a grid under the package instead of leads at the edge.
It packs a lot of pins into a small area, has short, low-inductance connections, good heat flow into the board and self-aligns during reflow.

The costs are hidden joints that need X-ray, rework stations and reballing, tough escape routing that can force via-in-pad and more layers at fine pitch, and thermal-cycling fatigue, worst at the corner balls.
I use them when pin count or speed demands it and plan the board and assembly for them."
